docs.title: rocm-bake
docs.text:
Reproducible builds of PyTorch, Triton, AITER, CuPy, NIXL, MORI, vLLM and LMCache against ROCm, on a three-node BuildKit fleet, with every artifact published to a local OCI registry.

The build is one docker buildx bake file and one Makefile. Everything else exists to make that build fast, repeatable and measurable.

docs.title: What It Builds
docs.text:
PyTorch from source against ROCm, with Triton, AITER, CuPy, NIXL, vLLM and LMCache on top, for gfx950 (default), gfx1201 and gfx1250. MORI builds alongside them as its own wheel and its own UMBP service image — see MORI and UMBP.

And two lanes that are tied to no architecture and need no GPU. One is a vLLM built with no device backend, which serves from a captured latency profile rather than a card — see emulated serving. The other is vLLM and LMCache built for CPU, which loads a small model and serves real tokens — see CPU serving. They are the only serving lanes here that are tested end to end: the first has timing and no tokens, the second tokens and no timing.

Every pinned version is on the bake variables page, generated from rocm-bake.hcl — the single source for every value a build reads. make list-vars prints what is in effect; make version-check compares it against upstream and against the published wheels.

docs.title: Live Reports
docs.text:
Two lanes publish measurements continuously. They are not comparable with each other — see Live reports.

  • Fleet Runs ↗

    Every wheel across all three SNOC nodes at once, instrumented. Newest run, with a selector for every earlier one. The same chart serves a run still in flight — make perf-serve.

  • Nightly Builds ↗

    One warm bake per architecture on AWS CodeBuild, 02:17 UTC, published to ECR.

A second lane builds on AWS CodeBuild each night — no fleet, no instances to own, $13.94 a run. See Building on AWS.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Commands run from the repository root on snoc-strix unless stated otherwise. make help lists every target; targets marked * build and push to the registry, which needs the ci login.

The repository is at sbates130272/rocm-bake and is MIT licensed.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: From nothing to a published PyTorch image. On a fleet that is already set up, skip to step 5.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The fleet below is manifests/snoc.yml, which is what FLEET defaults to. Everything here reads that file, so a different fleet is a different manifest rather than a different set of instructions — see The fleet.

  • All nodes on the same Tailscale network.
  • snoc-strix: a gfx1151 GPU, Docker 27+. Runs the Zot registry, the shared compiler cache, and the GPU tests.
  • snoc-thinkstation, snoc-gaming: Docker 27+, reachable as ssh <host> from Strix. Both are gfx1201 (RDNA4): they cross-compile for gfx950 fine but cannot run the test stage.
  • 200 GB+ of disk per node for the BuildKit cache.
docker --version
docker buildx version

The tailnet must bypass the corporate proxy

Every proxy-aware tool — curl, urllib, and the Go binaries including docker — tries to reach snoc-* through ZScaler and fails. The Makefile exports NO_PROXY_LIST for its own targets; anything run by hand needs the same in your shell profile:

export no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1,.ts.net,.local,10.0.0.0/8,100.64.0.0/10
export NO_PROXY="$no_proxy"

docs.title: Step 1 — Clone
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:sbates130272/rocm-bake.git
cd rocm-bake

docs.title: Step 2 — Check Zot
docs.text:
Zot is the local OCI registry: published images, the BuildKit layer cache as OCI artifacts, and a pull-through mirror of Docker Hub, GHCR and Quay. It runs on Strix as a bare-metal systemd service, deployed outside this repository.

Do not start a second one

Other services pull through the same registry. Nothing here starts, stops or configures Zot — the zot-* targets only inspect it.

make zot-check      # is it active and answering?
make zot-catalog    # what does it hold?

Anonymous read is open; only pushing needs the ci account. Store that credential with pass, which is GPG-encrypted at rest and works over SSH — the secretservice helper fails with Cannot create an item in a locked collection unless gnome-keyring has been unlocked graphically.

sudo apt-get install -y pass golang-docker-credential-helpers
pass init <your-gpg-key-id>        # gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
# set "credsStore": "pass" in ~/.docker/config.json
docker login snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080 -u ci
docker-credential-pass list        # verify it landed

One login on Strix covers the fleet: buildx sends registry auth to the builder as a session attachment.

Zot also needs a raised HTTP read timeout, or pushing the ROCm base fails — its largest layer is 8.67 GB and cannot cross a 1 Gb/s link inside Zot's 60-second default:

"http": {
  "readTimeout": "30m",
  "writeTimeout": "30m"
}

then sudo systemctl restart zot. Troubleshooting has what the failure looks like.

The registry serves plain HTTP over the tailnet, so the Docker daemon needs it in /etc/docker/daemon.json:

{
  "insecure-registries": ["snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080"],
  "registry-mirrors": ["http://snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080"]
}

make fleet-apply writes that file on every build node, from the manifest's registry.

docs.title: Step 3 — Create The Builders
docs.text:
make list-nodes             # which fleet this is, and what it declares
make builder-setup          # one builder per build node in the manifest
make builder-snoc-think     # or just one of them
make builder-status         # what exists now

There is no list of builders in the Makefile — builder-setup expands the manifest's node list. The remote nodes join over SSH to their Docker daemons, so neither needs buildkitd, TLS certificates or the plugin.

Every builder gets a buildkitd.toml rendered for that node and --driver-opt network=host. Both are load-bearing:

  • the config carries plain HTTP to Zot, the pull-through mirrors and a [dns] block — BuildKit writes its own resolv.conf and defaults it to 8.8.8.8, so without the block a RUN step cannot resolve any tailnet name;
  • network=host gives the builder the host's resolver, MagicDNS included, which Docker strips from a bridged container's.

Both are fixed at create time

An existing builder does not pick up a later change. Adopting one costs that node's BuildKit content store: docker buildx rm snoc-strix && make builder-snoc-strix.

docs.title: Step 4 — Deploy The Shared Compiler Cache
docs.text:
Every build container runs its own sccache server, all sharing one object store: nginx with the WebDAV modules on Strix at :8081. An object compiled on any node is a hit on the others.

sudo ./.builders/deploy-webdav.sh
make cache-check                 # can every node reach it?
make cache-summary               # endpoint, size, disk, deltas, hit rates

The port and path come from the manifest, so the deployer and the builders cannot disagree about where the store is. make fleet-check asks every node whether it can write to it, not just reach it: a node that can only read compiles everything and shares none of it, which looks exactly like a slow node.

Why a durable store, and why WebDAV

An in-RAM store loses the whole fleet's compiler cache on a power cycle; a plain directory tree survives and backs up with rsync. WebDAV rather than S3/MinIO because dl.min.io is blocked by the corporate proxy while nginx-extras is a normal apt install. Off the fleet, the nightly uses S3.

There is nothing to install on the other nodes.

docs.title: Step 5 — Build
docs.text:
make build-pytorch                    # one target on $(BUILDER)
make build-all                        # every target, one builder
make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool       # scheduled across all three nodes

BUILDER=snoc-pool is a sentinel, not a buildx builder: it routes through the balancer, one bake per target, results handed between nodes through Zot.

Each make build-* runs through telemetry/build.sh, which records duration, layer-cache hit ratio and sccache counters, then exits with the build's own status. TELEMETRY=0 skips it.

The build refuses to start when the compiler-cache store is unreachable, rather than silently recompiling everything:

docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0' pytorch

docs.title: Watch It
docs.text:
From a second terminal:

make build-watch                        # every builder, with a live tail
make build-watch WATCH_BUILDERS=snoc-think WATCH_LINES=40

Or one thing at a time:

make build-status     # records on $(BUILDER): running, completed, errored
make build-logs       # step output; BUILD=<id> for a specific record
make build-inspect    # duration, steps, cached steps, VCS revision
make builder-logs     # buildkitd's own log: registry, DNS, cache failures
make build-stop       # cancel builds started from this repo

build-logs is what the steps printed; builder-logs is the daemon underneath, where a registry, DNS or cache fault shows up while the build merely looks slow.

docs.title: Step 6 — Verify
docs.text:
make gpu-test GPU_HOST=snoc-thinkstation PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH=gfx1201

It checks per-dtype numerics on real hardware, and exists because a BuildKit RUN step has no /dev/kfd — an incorrect HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION once shipped undetected in every image.

By hand:

docker run --rm -it --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri \
  snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net:8080/rocm-pytorch/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx950

import torch
print(torch.__version__)           # 2.15.0a0+git31a77fc.rocm10.1.0
print(torch.cuda.is_available())   # True
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

docs.title: Step 7 — Measure It
docs.text:
make bench BENCH_SCENARIO=cold BUILDER=snoc-think
make bench-report

See Performance for what the four scenarios mean and how to read the numbers.

docs.title: Live Reports
docs.text:
Two lanes publish measurements continuously, to two pages on the gh-pages branch. Neither is committed to main — the data only exists where it was produced.

  • Fleet Runs — data/perf/

    Every wheel built across all three SNOC nodes at once, with CPU, memory, compiler-cache and registry traffic sampled throughout. Opens on the newest run, with a selector for every earlier one.

    Driven by hand with make perf-cold or make perf-warm, published with make perf-publish PUSH=1 from a build node. How it works.

  • Nightly Builds — data/nightly/

    One warm bake per architecture on a rented AWS CodeBuild machine, 02:17 UTC, published to ECR. Phase wall clock and cache-error counts, every run kept. A table, not a chart — see below.

    Fully automated, and it files a comment on one nightly-labelled issue as well. How it works, what it costs.

The two are not comparable

A fleet run is a parallel build across three nodes sharing a compiler cache. A nightly is sequential bakes on one rented machine, and its phase wall clock is the whole bake rather than a per-target cost. Quoting one as the other is the mistake both pages open by warning about.

A third set of numbers — isolated per-target costs under four cache conditions — lives on Performance, and is not comparable with either.

docs.title: Browsing Older Runs
docs.text:
Both pages keep everything ever published, and both open on the newest run — but they are not the same page, and only one of them charts.

data/perf/ is the interactive chart. perfsite.py writes a runs.json and a runs/<stamp>.json beside it, which the page fetches relative to its own URL to populate a selector; every run also keeps a data/perf/<stamp>/ permalink. Pick any past run from the dropdown and you get its full chart — overlaid CPU and memory, a legend that filters by builder and target, per-band hover.

data/nightly/ is a table, plus one bar chart. nightlysite.py writes a row per run and architecture — cold, warm, cost, sccache hit rate, layer-cache hits — with a data/nightly/<stamp>/ permalink and its own runs.json. Above the table, build-time.svg plots warm wall clock per night, one bar group per architecture. No legend filtering, no per-target spans, no sampled series.

The chart appears only once there are two runs to compare: one bar is not a series, and drawing it would imply a trend that cannot exist.

The sampled chart does not cover the AWS runs, and cannot

Not an oversight, and the distinction is narrower than "no chart". A rented CodeBuild machine has none of what the fleet chart is drawn from: there is no node_exporter on three nodes to sample into samples.jsonl, no per-target trace-<target>.json, and no Zot or nginx log to slice. None of that becomes available by wanting it.

What a nightly can see is its own wall clock, the instance it was billed on, and what its phase logs already printed — which is what build-time.svg and the cost and cache columns are drawn from, and nothing more. A nightly times bake invocations and claims nothing it cannot see.

nightlysite.py is deliberately a separate index for the same reason the admonition above gives. Merging the two selectors would put a parallel three-node run and a sequential one-machine run in the same dropdown, which is the not-comparable mistake made structural.

docs.title: Watching A Run Live
docs.text:
For fleet runs, the published page is not a different tool from the local one — perf-publish puts the chart perf-serve renders onto gh-pages and adds the cross-run selector. So the same interface works on a run that is still going:

make perf-serve             # newest run, http://<host>:8090
make perf-serve-status      # whether one is up, and where
make perf-serve-stop        # stop it, free PERF_PORT

It regenerates every 30 s and re-resolves which run is newest each cycle, so it picks up a run that starts after the server did. The page polls data.json rather than reloading, because the legend is the filter — a reload would discard whichever builders and targets you had narrowed to. A published run is frozen and stops polling.

perf-serve binds every interface

0.0.0.0 by default, because the usual viewer is a laptop on the LAN rather than on the tailnet. What that exposes is build telemetry — hostnames, CPU and memory figures, build step names — with no credentials and no registry access. Narrow it with PERF_BIND=<ip>, and make perf-serve-stop when you are done.

docs.title: What Each Publishes
docs.text:
Fleet runs Nightly Where data/perf/<stamp>/ data/nightly/<stamp>/<arch>/ Who runs it an operator, on demand schedule:, nightly Machines three, in parallel one, sequential Caches both live (warm) or neither (cold) registry + sccache on S3 Reports per-target spans, CPU/cache/registry traffic phase wall clock, cache errors Harness .builders/perfrun.sh .builders/nightly.sh Index perfsite.py — selector over every run nightlysite.py — one table of every run Older runs dropdown, plus <stamp>/ permalinks table rows, plus <stamp>/ permalinks Charted yes — CPU, memory, per-target spans no Live view make perf-serve —

The nightly skips itself when main has not moved since the last successful scheduled run, so a gap in the table is usually a quiet week rather than a failure.

docs.title: Installing The Wheels
docs.text:
Every architecture this repo builds has a public pip index. The wheels themselves are GitHub release assets; the index pages point at them, with a #sha256= on every link so pip verifies what it downloads.

Browse the indexes · Build performance

pip install \
  --index-url https://sbates130272.github.io/rocm-bake/data/wheels/gfx950/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  "rocm-torch[device-gfx950]"

Substitute gfx1201, gfx1151 or gfx1250 for another card. That installs the newest build on the newest ROCm, which is what most people want.

docs.title: Choosing A ROCm Version, Or A Build
docs.text:
Nothing that has been published is ever removed or replaced, so an install can be held still at either level.

A ROCm version. data/wheels/<arch>/ follows the newest ROCm published for that card. Each ROCm version also has an index of its own, which a newer ROCm never changes. Use it on a host whose ROCm is not the newest:

pip install \
  --index-url https://sbates130272.github.io/rocm-bake/data/wheels/rocm10.1/gfx950/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  "rocm-torch[device-gfx950]"

A build. Wheels are rebuilt weekly, and whenever a pin moves. Each build is a version of rocm-torch, and every build stays in its index, so pinning the metapackage pins the version of every wheel in the set:

pip install \
  --index-url https://sbates130272.github.io/rocm-bake/data/wheels/rocm10.2/gfx950/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  "rocm-torch[device-gfx950]==10.2.0.20261127"

The index pages list every build each index holds. Pin against the versioned path rather than the bare one: after the next ROCm release the bare path is a different index, and the build you named is not in it.

Builds published before 2026-11-20 have no build number. Their rocm-torch is 10.1.0+gfx950.6b049405, which ==10.1.0 selects.

A build pin selects versions, not bytes

Pinning a build fixes which version of each wheel is installed. It does not promise the bytes that build shipped. The builds are not bit-reproducible: two builds on the same pins produce a torch with the same filename and a different sha256 — measured on the first two gfx1201 builds for ROCm 10.2, where all ten wheels whose version was unchanged differed. An index can offer one file per filename, and it offers the newest. So an older build's rocm-torch installs today with the newer build's files wherever the version did not move.

For the exact files, record them: a lockfile or pip install --require-hashes holds each URL and hash, and those keep working because a published asset is never replaced. Every build's own files stay on its release page.

A week in which nothing changed publishes nothing. The build number is the date a set of wheels first differed from the one before it, not the date of a run.

No GPU? There is an emu index

One index is not a card: emu carries a vLLM built with no device backend at all, plus the emulator that makes it still serve. It installs anywhere and runs nothing on a GPU — see Emulated serving.

It is kept out of the per-card indexes on purpose. Two builds of vllm in one index would let pip hand the emulator to someone who asked for device-gfx950.

That index carries no torch and pins none, so installing from it is two steps — see Emulated serving.

No GPU, real inference: the cpu index

cpu carries vLLM and LMCache built for CPU, which serve real tokens from a small model. It is separate for the same reason, and its metapackage is still rocm-torch[device-cpu]. Not published yet: the index URL returns 404 until the first make cpu-publish.

Its vLLM pins torch==2.15.0+cpu, so torch is installed first from PyTorch's CPU index and that index is given again as a second --extra-index-url. pip only: uv refuses the wheel's direct-URL triton requirement. The exact lines are in CPU serving.

Both index URLs are required

--extra-index-url is not optional. Ordinary dependencies — numpy, pydantic, a hundred others — live on PyPI and the install cannot resolve without it. --index-url must stay first: it is the one that carries our wheels.

docs.title: What rocm-torch Is
docs.text:
A generated metapackage. It carries no code; it pins every wheel in one architecture's index at the exact version built against that ROCm and that torch:

torch==2.15.0a0+git31a77fc.rocm10.1.0; extra == "device-gfx950"
atom==0.1.9+rocm10.1.0;                extra == "device-gfx950"
...

Installing it is how you get a set that was built together rather than a set pip assembled. The exact pins are also the defence against name collisions — see below.

Its own version looks like 10.2.0.20261127+gfx950.424e84fe: the ROCm version, the build number, the architecture, and a digest of the pin set. The digest moves whenever the pinned versions do, so a rebuild is a new version rather than the same version with different contents, which a pip cache is entitled to assume. The build number is what orders them: a digest says two builds differ and not which is newer, so without it "the latest rocm-torch" in an index holding several would be whichever digest sorted last.

Everything after the + is ignored by a pin that does not mention it, which is why ==10.2.0.20261127 is enough to name a build.

docs.title: Reading A Version
docs.text:
A version string says which ROCm the wheel was built against.

wheel version platform tag torch 2.15.0a0+git31a77fc.rocm10.1.0 linux_x86_64 triton 3.9.0+gitaad2a60d.rocm10.1.0 linux_x86_64 amd_aiter 0.1.29.dev0+g…d20261109.rocm10.1.0 linux_x86_64 cupy 14.2.0+rocm10.1.0 manylinux_2_39 lmcache 0.5.6+rocm10.1.0 manylinux_2_39 atom 0.1.9+rocm10.1.0 manylinux_2_38 torchvision 0.29.2+rocm10.1.0 manylinux_2_39 amd_mori 1.2.3.post1+rocm10.2.0 manylinux_2_39 nixl 1.5.2+rocm10.1.0 py3-none-any nixl_rocm 1.5.2+rocm10.1.0 manylinux_2_39 vllm 0.33.0+rocm101 linux_x86_64 triton_kernels 1.0.0 py3-none-any

Where a wheel already carried a git hash, the ROCm marker is appended to it rather than replacing it, so the commit stays visible. vllm carries upstream's own +rocm101. triton_kernels is pure Python with no ROCm code to qualify.

Nothing in a filename says which GPU

torch for gfx950 and for gfx1201 is the same filename and the two files differ by about 40MB of device code. The architecture is carried by the index path and by the metapackage, which is why downloading a release asset by hand is not a supported way to install these. Use the index.

docs.title: Why Some Wheels Are manylinux And Others Are Not
docs.text:
A manylinux_X_Y tag is a verified promise: this loads on any glibc at or above X.Y. auditwheel grants one only by reading the compiled code and taking the newest glibc symbol it references — so the tag depends on what the code calls, not on what machine built it. It is measured here, never asserted.

  • cupy, lmcache, atom, torchvision, nixl_rocm, amd_mori fall inside a policy auditwheel defines. Their non-system dependencies are vendored into the wheel and the tag is rewritten to match.
  • torch, triton, vllm cannot have one. They reference symbols newer than any policy auditwheel knows — torch needs GLIBC_2.43, the base image's glibc — so auditwheel show ends at "This constrains the platform tag to linux_x86_64". No exclude list changes that; the symbol is in torch's own code.
  • amd_aiter has nothing to describe. At PREBUILD_KERNELS=0 it contains no x86_64 ELF at all, only GPU code objects, and auditwheel refuses it outright. It is still architecture-specific — for the GPU, which no platform tag can express.

Everything ROCm ships is excluded from vendoring, because the consuming environment is expected to have the same ROCm these were built against. A wheel carrying its own copy of hipBLAS or RCCL would both be enormous and shadow the runtime everything else is using.

A manylinux tag says nothing about ROCm's bundled libraries

Excluding a soname tells auditwheel both do not vendor this and do not count it against the policy. So a wheel can be manylinux_2_39 and still need a library from the ROCm tree.

amd_mori is where this first bit. Its UMBP binaries link librocm_sysdeps_z.so.1 and librocm_sysdeps_numa.so.1 — ROCm's renamed copies of zlib and libnuma — and that directory, /opt/rocm/lib/rocm_sysdeps/lib, is on no loader path by default: no ld.so.conf.d entry, not in LD_LIBRARY_PATH, invisible to ldconfig. ROCm's own libraries find it through $ORIGIN RPATHs; a binary built outside that tree does not. The mori image adds the ld.so.conf.d entry, so installing that image is fine; installing the wheel alone into an arbitrary ROCm environment may not be.

docs.title: Name Collisions With PyPI
docs.text:
Several of these names are also published by someone else, and pip has no notion of "prefer this index". It picks by version.

That is a real failure mode here, not a theoretical one. nixl is also NVIDIA's, at the same upstream version: their nixl 1.5.2 is a CUDA meta-package whose hard dependencies are nixl-cu12 and nixl-cu13. With both at 1.5.2 pip had no tiebreaker and took theirs — so a ROCm index installed CUDA backends. The same shape applies to atom, which is Nucleic's Atom framework on PyPI at a much higher version, and to torch, where PyPI's final 2.15.0 outranks our 2.15.0a0 alpha.

The local version segment is what resolves all of them. +rocm10.1.0 cannot be matched by an upstream release, so a metapackage pin of nixl==1.5.2+rocm10.1.0 is unsatisfiable by NVIDIA's 1.5.2 and ours is the only candidate. This is why installing the metapackage, rather than the individual wheels, is the supported path — the exact pins are the mechanism.

A scheduled workflow re-resolves every published index weekly and fails if any of our distributions comes from PyPI or any CUDA package appears, because this class of breakage arrives without a commit of ours: it starts the day somebody else publishes a colliding name.

docs.title: What The Index Promises
docs.text:
• A published file never changes. Each build is its own GitHub release, tagged wheels-<rocm>-<arch>-<build>, and nothing is uploaded over an existing asset or deleted from one. A URL and the sha256 beside it mean the same bytes for as long as they exist, so a lockfile that recorded them keeps working.
  • A filename appears once. A wheel that two builds share byte for byte is listed at the URL it was first published under. Where two builds have the same filename and different bytes — a rebuild at an unchanged version, which is the usual case — the newest is listed. The older file is still on its release, and no longer in the index.
  • Dependencies resolve without downloading wheels. Each wheel's metadata is served beside it (PEP 658), so an installer reads a few KB to plan an install instead of fetching torch to find out what it requires. Each link also carries the wheel's Requires-Python.
  • The index can be rebuilt from the releases. Every release carries a manifest.json describing its build, and make wheels-reindex regenerates every index page from those. The pages on gh-pages are a rendering, not a record.

docs.title: Python Version
docs.text:
The wheels are cp314. Ubuntu 26.04 is the only base AMD publishes ROCm 10.1 for and it ships no other Python, so there is no other build.

Nothing in the set caps below 3.14, so the full install needs no special flags. make wheel-index measures each wheel's Requires-Python and names any that excludes the interpreter here, so if an upstream does cap it shows up as a note rather than an opaque resolution failure.

docs.title: Node Roles
docs.text:
snoc-strix is the default BUILDER and hosts both shared services. Its GPU is gfx1151; no node has a gfx950 card, which is the default build target, so make test only proves anything when PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH matches the hardware it runs on.

snoc-think and snoc-gaming are build capacity, joined to buildx over SSH to their Docker daemons, so neither needs buildkitd, TLS certificates or the plugin. Both are gfx1201 (RDNA4) and cross-compile for gfx950 without difficulty, but cannot run the test stage.

snoc-pool is a sentinel, not a node: it routes through .builders/balance.sh rather than to a buildx builder. See the balancer.

docs.title: Why A Tailnet
docs.text:
The three machines are not on one LAN, and the corporate proxy must never see tailnet traffic. Two consequences run through everything else:

  • no_proxy has to include .ts.net or every proxy-aware tool fails against snoc-*. The Makefile exports it; interactive shells need it in a profile.
  • Name resolution inside a build container is not the node's. BuildKit writes its own resolv.conf and defaults it to a public resolver, so .builders/buildkitd.toml.in carries a [dns] block listing MagicDNS first and two public resolvers after. The public entries are load-bearing: this tailnet has no global nameservers, so MagicDNS SERVFAILs on anything outside it and apt, pip and the PyTorch clone would all fail.

Even that was not enough for the compiler cache. Under load a tailnet lookup falls through to a public resolver, which answers NXDOMAIN, the search domain is appended, and the query becomes snoc-strix.fold-leaffish.ts.net.fold-leaffish.ts.net — 79 of 361 compiles lost in one Triton build. So the Makefile resolves the store's hostname once on the host, and build containers address it by IP.

docs.title: Single Source Of Truth
docs.text:
rocm-bake.hcl owns every value a build reads. The Makefile keeps no copy: it parses the variable blocks at parse time and reads the defaults out. The two used to disagree silently — a make target and a bare docker buildx bake built different images from the same tree, and nothing said so.

.builders/check-defaults.py enforces it in CI, failing the build if a default is re-declared in the Makefile, if the Makefile reads a variable that does not exist, if $(call bake,…) names a missing target, or if WHEEL_REPOS drifts from the wheels group. The same pattern applies to serving/docker-compose.yml, which owns the runtime defaults.

docs.title: ATOM and vLLM: the skew, and what checks it
docs.text: ATOM ships a vLLM V1 platform plugin. This repo builds both. They are pinned independently, they move independently, and until now nothing in either tree noticed when they moved apart.

docs.title: The problem, stated precisely
docs.text:
ATOM_REF = v0.1.10 declares its target vLLM in atom/plugin/vllm/vllm-version.env:

VLLM_COMMIT=db9527a46873454610df6dbedf79a36d6bf1a7f6
VLLM_VERSION=0.31.0

VLLM_REF = v0.34.0. Three minor releases apart. (v0.1.10 left that file byte-identical to v0.1.9's, so the skew only widened.)

Everything measured below was measured against vLLM v0.33.0, when this repo pinned it. The pin has since moved to v0.34.0 and those symbol-level findings have not been re-measured against it; the gate in docker/Dockerfile.atom-vllm is what re-runs on every build.

Nothing catches that. There is no reference to vllm.__version__ anywhere under ATOM's atom/, and ATOM's pyproject.toml declares no vllm dependency at all, so pip installs any pairing happily. Meanwhile the plugin makes ~320 import sites across 150 distinct private vLLM symbols and monkeypatches 48 call sites, almost all into vllm.v1.*.

Installing the ATOM wheel next to vLLM is enough to arm it. ATOM's pyproject.toml declares two entry points vLLM discovers automatically:

[project.entry-points."vllm.platform_plugins"]  atom = ...:register_platform
[project.entry-points."vllm.general_plugins"]   atom_model_registry = ...:register_model

so there is no "install it and decide later".

docs.title: Three failure modes, in rising order of nastiness
docs.text:
Loud. A symbol moved, the import raises, somebody reads a traceback.

Silent — the module survived and its contents did not. vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_utils still exists at 0.33. All seven functions ATOM monkeypatches onto it (get_kv_cache_groups, get_kv_cache_config_from_groups, _max_memory_usage_bytes_from_groups, _pool_bytes_per_block, get_kv_cache_configs, _auto_fit_max_model_len, may_override_num_blocks) moved to vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_planning. An installer guarded by try: import ... except ImportError sails straight through, finds nothing to patch, and returns. ATOM v0.1.9 has two such installers: one raises AttributeError at startup, the other uses getattr(module, name, None) and simply does not install — leaving DeepSeek V4.1's --max-model-len -1 to fit against a pool whose STATE tail has not been taken out yet. No error. Wrong number.

Silent and arithmetic. _pool_bytes_per_block both moved and gained a vllm_config first parameter. Fix only the path and the call passes the groups list where the config belongs, raises nothing, and returns wrong bytes-per-block.

ATOM's own register.py documents an instance of the second kind in its own history: "the dummy-run marking once covered nothing while the synthetic batches went on taking real STATE slots."

docs.title: What checks it now
docs.text:
Two tools, in the ATOM fork (sbates130272/ATOM, branch v0.1.9-vllm0.33), both upstreamable as-is.

compat_check doctor asks can the symbol be found? did the patch actually go in? method AST on both sides, no import runs both registration hooks needs nothing — no vLLM, torch, GPU the whole stack, a GPU runs in the atom-vllm build, in CI make atom-vllm-doctor misses patches that stand down symbols it never reaches

compat_check reports four things and exits non-zero on any of them: unresolved imports (counting try/except ImportError ladders as one group, and skipping if TYPE_CHECKING: blocks, which never execute); monkeypatch targets that no longer exist; the state of every entry in the relocation table; and arity drift on relocated symbols.

That last pair is the forward-looking half. Once a call site is rewritten to go through the shim it contains no from vllm... import for a scanner to find, so the table is resolved directly — otherwise the check would go quiet on exactly the symbols most likely to move again.

doctor prints one row per patch: installed, stood down with a reason, or raised. It exits non-zero when a patch did not install and gave no reason.

docs.title: Where it is wired in
docs.text:
• ATOM_REPO (rocm-bake.hcl) selects which ATOM to build. Upstream by default. Pair it with an ATOM_REF that is a tag on the fork — the clone in Dockerfile.atom is layer-cached on the ref string, so a branch name builds once and then never updates.
  • atom-vllm (docker/Dockerfile.atom-vllm) is the vLLM image with the ATOM wheel installed and compat_check run against it as a build gate. A future VLLM_REF bump that moves a symbol fails that build with a named list. It needs no GPU, so it runs on the fleet and on CodeBuild alike.
  • make atom-vllm-doctor is the on-hardware half, run deliberately.

The plugin ships disabled (ATOM_DISABLE_VLLM_PLUGIN=1). Enabling it replaces vLLM's model classes for 30 architectures.

docs.title: What none of this establishes
docs.text: That a model generates tokens through the plugin. ATOM's kernels need gfx942, gfx950 or gfx1250; manifests/snoc.yml has gfx1151 and gfx1201 and nothing else. A clean compat_check means nothing will fail to import. A clean doctor means the patches installed. Neither is evidence about numerics, and the gap is not closable on this fleet.

docs.title: LMCache MP, since it comes up
docs.text:
Three separate things get conflated:

  1. ATOM's own lmcache_mp connector is not reachable from plugin mode. It is registered in ATOM's connector factory and serves the native engine; in plugin mode vLLM resolves connectors through its own registry, where ATOM exposes only AtomLMCacheOffloadConnector. ATOM says so itself in atom/plugin/vllm/platform.py.
  2. The cupy blocker ATOM documents is stale. The connector docstring says LMCache's ROCm platform does not provide cupy. At LMCache v0.5.6 RocmDeviceSpec subclasses CudaDeviceSpec and inherits the cupy cache context; cupy maps launch_host_func to hipLaunchHostFunc for HIP >= 5.4 (we are on ROCm 10.1); and this repo already builds that ROCm cupy wheel. The default IPC path is PyTorch storage IPC, not cupy IPC.
  3. LMCache v0.5.6 imports clean against vLLM 0.33.0. Measured with the same checker pointed at it: 79 import sites, 53 distinct symbols, one unresolved — vllm.attention:Attention in a FlashInfer module never loaded on ROCm.

The real constraint is layout, not version. LMCache's GPU connectors take one clean NHD/HND format for the whole model; ATOM's plugin-mode KV tensors for MLA/DSA models are not that, which is why ATOM wrote its own byte-codec connector. So LMCache MP alongside the ATOM plugin is sound for models whose ATOM layout is plain NHD/HND and unsound for MLA/M3/DSA ones — and that is true of 0.31 and 0.33 equally.

docs.title: AITER
docs.text:
ATOM declares no aiter constraint either — no version, no range, ~700 call sites. compat_check --package aiter covers it with the same code, and the atom-vllm build runs it. Not as a gate yet: it has never been measured, so the first findings are information rather than grounds to fail a vLLM build.

The v0.1.28 -> v0.1.28.post1 bump does not change any of this. It touches aiter/ops/topk_select.py, but only to widen _SUPPORTED_GFX from ("gfx942", "gfx950", "gfx1250") to add "gfx1250-strict". Still no RDNA, so docker/atom-topk-fallback.py and its reasoning stand unchanged.

    vllmw["vllm-wheel"]
    mori["mori<br/><i>UMBP runtime image</i>"]
    moriw["mori-wheel"]

    rocm --> base
    src --> pt
    src --> ptw
    rocm --> run
    base --> triton
    base --> cupy
    base --> pt
    triton --> pt
    pt --> ptw

Six edges are not obvious from the names.

triton-wheel builds from the base, not from pytorch. Triton needs cmake<4 while PyTorch pulls cmake 4.x, so they cannot share an environment — which also lets Triton build in parallel with PyTorch. It is the only target with no architecture in its tag.

cupy-wheel hangs off the base too, because CuPy has no torch dependency. It is not optional: LMCache's MP server imports cupy at module scope, no published wheel fits this stack, and without it the server dies on the first request while vLLM waits five minutes before reporting a generic engine failure.

mori hangs off the base and nothing consumes it. MORI is built with BUILD_TORCH_SYMM=OFF, so it needs no torch and sits beside cupy-wheel rather than behind the PyTorch compile. Nothing points out of it either: UMBP runs as its own multi-process service, so the image is a leaf rather than an input to vllm. See MORI and UMBP.

vllm consumes lmcache-wheel. vLLM ships the LMCache MP connector but imports lmcache.utils from it, so the wheel must exist first — and on the scheduled path, be published first.

lmcache takes no AITER context: its extension is cache movement, not GEMMs.

vllm consumes torchvision-wheel, which looks like an optional extra and is not. vLLM's build requirements pull timm, timm requires torchvision, and transformers' image_utils imports torchvision.io at module scope. PyPI publishes only CUDA builds of it, so without this edge the serving image carries a torchvision that cannot load on ROCm. It hangs off pytorch because its setup.py imports torch to decide it is building for ROCm at all — which is also why it cannot be installed into pytorch itself.

Group Members default rocm-runtime, pytorch-src, pytorch-base, pytorch, pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, torchvision-wheel, atom-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel, mori, mori-wheel wheels pytorch-wheel, triton-wheel, aiter-wheel, nixl-wheel, torchvision-wheel, atom-wheel, cupy-wheel, vllm-wheel, lmcache-wheel, mori-wheel serving torchvision-wheel, cupy-wheel, nixl-wheel, vllm, vllm-wheel, lmcache, lmcache-wheel

There is no all group. Two targets are deliberately outside default:

  • pytorch-run is excluded because no node has a usable GPU to exercise it on. make push-runtime still builds it.

docs.title: How Inputs Are Wired
docs.text:
Targets take their inputs from siblings through target: named contexts — bake's dependency mechanism, and the only one it has.

contexts = USE_PUB ? {} : {
  triton-wheels = "target:triton-wheel"
  base-img      = "target:pytorch-base"
}
args = {
  TRITON_WHEEL_IMAGE = USE_PUB ? PUB_TRITON : "triton-wheels"
  BASE_IMAGE         = USE_PUB ? PUB_BASE   : "base-img"
}

A target with no context on its inputs is, as far as bake is concerned, independent — and may run concurrently with the thing it needs.

docs.title: PUBLISHED_INPUTS
docs.text:
Set PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 and every one of those contexts collapses to a registry reference; the PUB_* locals hold them and must track the tags of the target they mirror.

This is what makes cross-node scheduling possible: a target: context only works within one bake invocation, so one-bake-per-node would rebuild the whole chain rather than pulling what the previous stage pushed. pytorch-run is the exception — its context must resolve in both modes, so it uses docker-image://.

Note

PUBLISHED_INPUTS is read by bake from the environment, so it needs PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1 make …, not make … PUBLISHED_INPUTS=1. Same for SCCACHE_LOG, RUN_ID, CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX and the SDE_* overrides.

docs.title: The Balancer
docs.text:
buildx's multi-node builder does not balance: selection is by platform match, so when every node advertises linux/amd64 the choice ignores capacity — all five targets once landed on snoc-gaming (16 cores, 15 GB) while snoc-think (32 cores, 122 GB) sat idle. There is no hook to change it, so scheduling happens in .builders/balance.sh instead, one bake invocation per target pinned to a builder it picks.

make push-all BUILDER=snoc-pool       # the usual way to build everything
make push-wheels BUILDER=snoc-pool    # just the wheel artifacts
.builders/balance.sh --dry-run        # what it would schedule, and where
.builders/balance.sh --best           # the strongest node right now

Nodes are scored by free GB of RAM plus idle cores, weighted equally on purpose: a cold PyTorch runs one cc1plus per core at 1–2 GB each, so RAM is what bounds a big node.

Work is scheduled from the dependency graph, not a list kept beside it. .builders/depgraph.py asks bake for each target's contexts, and balance.sh starts a target once every dependency inside the run has finished and been pushed, so what to build is a set (TARGETS="pytorch-wheel triton-wheel" .builders/balance.sh).

This replaced a hand-written STAGE_1..STAGE_5 — a second copy of what rocm-bake.hcl already stated, which drifted: a gfx1250 run scheduled vllm-wheel when no gfx1250 pytorch image existed, and died resolving it 0 s in, taking the rest of its node's queue with it.

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
Before any build starts, every image the run resolves from the registry — minus the ones it publishes itself — is checked against Zot, so a missing input is named up front with the make target that creates it, rather than killing a target at step 1 after work is committed.

depgraph: these images are needed but not published, and nothing in
this run builds them:
  …/rocm-pytorch/pytorch:2.15.0-10.1.0-full-gfx1250
      needed by: aiter-wheel, lmcache-wheel, nixl-wheel,
                 torchvision-wheel, vllm-wheel
   build it with: make push-pytorch

Only a 404 counts as absent: the corporate proxy answers 403 for the tailnet unless no_proxy covers it.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text: Among the targets eligible at any moment, the longest goes to the node that would finish it soonest, one build per node — several concurrent builds on one box each derive MAX_JOBS from MemAvailable as though alone, and oversubscribe it. The cost model is target-costs plus each node's link_mbps from the fleet manifest, ranked on finishing soonest rather than least loaded because this fleet's upload speeds span a factor of 25.

docs.title: Why build-all Refuses The Pool
docs.text:
make build-all BUILDER=snoc-pool errors rather than scheduling: every target would be its own bake invocation, so stage 2 would silently build against whatever is in the registry rather than what stage 1 produced. On a single builder the contexts resolve in-process and it is fine.

make push-all  BUILDER=snoc-pool    # scheduled, publishes
make build-all BUILDER=snoc-think   # single builder, no push

docs.title: MAX_JOBS
docs.text: Left empty, each build derives its job count from MemAvailable at 2 GB per job, sampled when the compile step starts — by which point its own earlier steps have taken memory. A cold PyTorch that settled at 21 GB derived 5 jobs where the same node gives a hot run 10, which is why the benchmark harness keys its results by job count.

docs.title: Telling Builds Apart
docs.text:
Every target stamps rocm-pytorch-build/<target>/<arch>/<RUN_ID> into its BuildKit history record. RUN_ID defaults to dev.

The prefix is this repository's name because a sibling project builds on the same nodes with the same convention and the same image names, and a shared prefix made its builds indistinguishable from these in make watch.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Four caches sit between a make build-pytorch and a from-scratch compile, and they are independent: a Dockerfile edit can drop layer reuse to 5% while sccache still serves every compile, and a changed compiler flag does the opposite.

flowchart LR
    build["a build step"]
    local["<b>1. BuildKit content store</b><br/>per node, local disk<br/>gckeepstorage 100GB"]
    layer["<b>2. Layer cache</b><br/>OCI artifacts in Zot<br/>two-tier: rolling + -ref"]
    sccache["<b>3. sccache</b><br/>nginx WebDAV on Strix :8081<br/>object files, fleet-wide"]
    pull["<b>4. Pull-through</b><br/>Zot mirrors Docker Hub,<br/>GHCR and Quay"]

    build --> local --> layer
    build --> sccache
    build --> pull

Each is removed by a different lever, which is what the benchmark scenarios are built on.

docs.title: 1. The Node's Content Store
docs.text: BuildKit keeps every blob it has pulled or produced on the node's disk, bounded by buildkit.gc_keep_storage in the fleet manifest. docker buildx prune is the only lever, and it is shared with any other project on that node.

docs.title: 2. The Layer Cache, In Zot
docs.text:
Each target exports its layers as OCI artifacts to a *-cache repository in Zot, so a layer built on one node is reusable from any of them.

Target Cache Repository rocm-runtime rocm-runtime-cache pytorch-base base-cache pytorch, pytorch-wheel pytorch-cache triton-wheel triton-wheel-cache aiter-wheel aiter-wheel-cache torchvision-wheel torchvision-wheel-cache pytorch-run runtime-cache cupy-wheel cupy-wheel-cache nixl-wheel nixl-wheel-cache vllm, vllm-wheel vllm-cache lmcache, lmcache-wheel lmcache-cache mori, mori-wheel mori-cache

docs.title: Two Tiers
docs.text: Reads always consult two refs: the rolling tag, and a frozen -ref baseline. Writes go to the rolling tag unless CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX=-ref (CACHE_TAG_SUFFIX=-ref make push-pytorch), which is how the baseline is deliberately refreshed. Without the second tier, one bad build overwrites the only cache everyone reads.

docs.title: Scoped By Architecture
docs.text:
Image tags have carried the architecture since ARCH_TAG landed; the cache refs did not. A gfx1201 build overwrote the gfx950 cache with layers gfx950 can never hit, and the next gfx950 build rebuilt cold and did the same back — so alternating architectures cost two cold builds, every time. CACHE_ARCH scopes those refs now.

triton-wheel stays on the shared ref deliberately: Triton is a compiler that publishes one noarch wheel. pytorch-base used to, and no longer does — it builds FROM rocm-runtime, whose kernel libraries are for one card, so one arch reading another's cache would take the wrong ones as a hit.

The unqualified base tag is no longer written

base:${ROCM_VERSION}-${PYTHON_VERSION} was published once for the whole fleet and is now ...-${ARCH_TAG}. Anything pinning the old form keeps resolving to the last image written under it, which gets staler from here. See Build targets.

Arch-sensitive targets also read the old unscoped latest, kept transitionally; it goes once each architecture has been built once.

Cache exports fail silently

Every cache-to carries ignore-error=true. A registry that is down, full, or refusing the push does not fail the build — it just means the next build has nothing to read. make builder-logs is where that shows up; the build itself only looks slow next time.

make layer-summary    # per image, most recent build, with the node it ran on
make build-inspect    # one build: duration, steps, cached steps

docs.title: 3. The Compiler Cache
docs.text:
Every build container runs its own sccache server, all sharing one object store: nginx with the WebDAV modules at /var/cache/sccache-webdav on Strix, port 8081. An object compiled on any node is a hit on the others.

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT     http://<resolved-ip>:8081
SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX   rocm-pytorch
SCCACHE_SERVER_UDS          /tmp/sccache.sock
CMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER   sccache
CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER sccache
CMAKE_HIP_COMPILER_LAUNCHER sccache
HIP_CLANG_LAUNCHER          /usr/local/bin/sccache

Off the fleet the same cache runs on S3 — SCCACHE_BUCKET outranks the WebDAV endpoint, and an empty bucket name is treated as unset. See Building on AWS.

Three constraints make this work, and each fails quietly if broken.

A shared server is impossible. sccache's client sends a path, and the server reads and hashes the file itself — so a server on the host cannot see a build container's sources. Only storage can be shared.

The server is addressed over a unix socket, not a TCP port. The builders run with network=host, so a fixed port would be shared fleet-wide: a Triton build's client once connected to a concurrent PyTorch build's server, which could not see the files it was asked to hash. There is deliberately no port variable.

The store is addressed by IP, not by name — see the tailnet DNS problem. The Makefile resolves the host once, so setting SCCACHE_WEBDAV_ENDPOINT yourself only affects a bare bake.

docs.title: Refusing To Build Uncached
docs.text:
docker/Dockerfile.pytorch probes the store at image build time and refuses to start a compile when it is unreachable, rather than spending an hour rebuilding everything:

docker buildx bake -f rocm-bake.hcl --set '*.args.REQUIRE_SCCACHE=0' pytorch

The build prints sccache --show-stats as its last action, which is where the telemetry wrapper reads the counters — they cannot be queried afterwards, since the server dies with the build container.

docs.title: Inspecting The Store
docs.text:
make cache-summary    # endpoint, size, disk, deltas, hit rates
make cache-check      # can every build node reach it?
make cache-logs       # the WebDAV access log

cache-summary prints a delta and a rate as well as totals, because "+412 objects" means something very different over eight seconds than over an hour. The hit rate comes from the telemetry textfile, not the store: WebDAV has no stats verb.

SCCACHE_WEBDAV_KEY_PREFIX is a directory in the store, so an experiment can run against an isolated namespace and delete it afterwards — which is what the benchmark harness does for its frozen and cold runs.

docs.title: Why Not Distributed Compilation
docs.text:
sccache has a second, separate feature: sccache-dist, a scheduler plus build servers that ship individual preprocessed compile jobs to other machines. It is orthogonal to the shared store above — a fleet would run both, not one instead of the other. We do not run it, and the reasoning is recorded here so the question does not have to be re-opened from scratch.

It is not a fleet balancer, and could not replace one. Its unit of work is a single object file. balance.sh schedules bake targets: a clone, apt, pip, cmake, the compile, wheel packaging, the layer export and a registry push. Most of what it schedules around is not compilation at all, and target-costs says so in measured numbers — pytorch-src is 1260s of almost pure network, rocm-runtime is I/O with no compiler in it, and torchvision-wheel is 27s of build against 2.6 GB of export. The export term that balance.sh charges against each node's link_mbps is invisible to sccache-dist. Adopting it would add a scheduler beside the one we have rather than removing it.

On a warm build there is nothing to distribute. Distribution only does work on a miss. The best recorded nightly ran 4494 requests for 4129 hits and 116 misses — 97.3 %, measured in the AWS analysis. A scheduler, build servers and a sandbox, to parallelise 116 compiles.

The one case where it would pay is cold. Packing runs one build per node, so once the short targets drain, the nodes that finished sit idle while pytorch-wheel runs alone — at 2336s against a ~5232s total, it is the makespan lower bound, and no amount of target-level packing can go below it. Splitting that one target's compiles across the idle nodes is the only thing that breaks that floor. But it only bites when the objects are genuinely missing: a version bump, a compiler-flag change, a FORCE_RECACHE run. At the current cadence those are the rare nights, and --skip-cold means most nightlies never see one.

So the precondition for revisiting is a change in that ratio — cold or bump builds becoming routine rather than exceptional, or a measurement showing the cold critical path costs more than the operational price below.

ROCm makes that price higher than the quickstart suggests

HIP compiles reach sccache through clang.rs, which does emit a distributable command — unlike nvcc.rs, which returns None and cannot be distributed at all. But --hip-path and --hip-device-lib-path are PassThroughPath: sccache packages the compiler by scanning its shared libraries, and the device bitcode is not a shared library. Every build server would need the identical ROCm tree at identical paths, matching the version pinned in the image — which is the one thing our containers exist to avoid depending on. On top of that the build servers want bubblewrap and run as root on bare metal, while our compiles happen inside BuildKit containers.

docs.title: 4. Pull-Through
docs.text:
.builders/buildkitd.toml.in points docker.io, ghcr.io and quay.io at Zot, which syncs them on demand. The ROCm base image is 8.67 GB in a single layer, so this is the difference between a build that starts in seconds and one that starts after a WAN transfer — which is what the frozen scenario measures.

What each cache is worth has a measured answer rather than an estimated one: see Performance.

docs.title: CPU Serving: Real Tokens, No GPU
docs.text:
The ROCm serving stack needs a card. The emulated one needs none, but loads no weights and emits a filler token. This lane is the one in between: vLLM and LMCache built for CPU, serving a real model, with weights loaded, a real forward pass, and KV blocks that go to LMCache and come back.

make cpu-load      # build both images into the local docker daemon
make cpu-test      # serve a model, check the answer and the cache

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Two images and two wheels, the bake group cpu, from docker/Dockerfile.vllm-cpu and docker/Dockerfile.lmcache-cpu: vLLM v0.33.0 built with VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu, LMCache v0.5.7 built with NO_GPU_EXT=1, both on torch==2.15.0+cpu. No ROCm, NIXL, CuPy, AITER or ATOM anywhere in it, and no ${ARCH} in any tag.

emu cpu ROCm (vllm, lmcache) Loads weights no yes yes Real tokens no — a fixed filler token yes yes Device latency replayed from a profile pack none real KV blocks through LMCache no yes yes Needs a card no no yes Tested end to end yes, in CI yes, in CI not in CI — make serve-test on a GPU node

So the two GPU-free lanes are complements. emu has timing and no tokens; this has tokens and no timing. Neither says anything about a ROCm kernel.

docs.title: How It Is Built
docs.text:
The non-obvious parts:

  • No ISA flag, because there is none to set. At this ref the x86 build always compiles three variants of its kernels with fixed flags — _C (AVX-512 + BF16 + VNNI + AMX), _C_AVX512 and _C_AVX2 — and picks one at runtime from CPUID. Nothing is -march=native. The floor is AVX2. The build asserts all three are in the wheel, and the image build loads _C_AVX2 by name and computes with it.
  • numactl-devel is the one thing the manylinux base lacks. Without it the build stops at fatal error: numa.h: No such file or directory. auditwheel repair then grafts libnuma into the wheel, which is not optional: python:3.14-slim has no system copy.
  • torch is consumed, not built. The lane's point is to need nothing from the fleet, and PyTorch publishes 2.15.0+cpu for cp314. Both wheels pin it: vLLM's requirements/cpu.txt is moved from 2.14.0+cpu, and LMCache's bare torch — which alone resolves PyPI's CUDA build, under extensions that link libtorch_cpu — becomes torch==2.15.0+cpu. The build fails if either sed matches nothing.
  • The version keeps +cpu. It is how vLLM selects CpuPlatform; the image build asserts that with VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE unset, which is how an installed wheel runs. Every other platform imports vllm._C unconditionally (read from source), and that extension is a SIGILL — not an ImportError — without AVX-512 (measured on the bare extension under qemu, not through the package). The image sets VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu as well. LMCache is versioned 0.5.7+cpu to match. Note vllm.__version__ says 0.33.0; the suffix is in the distribution version (vllm --version).
  • No Rust frontend. With no rustc on PATH, setup.py skips the optional vllm-rs binary.
  • The runtime image carries g++ (+277 MB). vLLM's CPU path compiles at serve time. With no compiler the default mode dies in warmup (InvalidCxxCompiler: No working C++ compiler found), and --enforce-eager only moves the failure to the first request (Failed to find C compiler, HTTP 500).
  • vLLM and LMCache are installed in one resolve. One after the other, LMCache's opentelemetry-api<=1.40 cap leaves pip check failing.

docs.title: The connector on CPU
docs.text:
serving/docker-compose.cpu.yml passes the bare "kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector". With LMCache installed vLLM resolves that to LMCache's own class (Using external LMCacheMPConnector); no kv_connector_module_path is needed. Measured on a repeated 1280-token prefix:

Configuration Result TRANSFER_MODE=lmcache_driven (default) works — stored in 0.021 s, retrieved in 0.014 s; moves vLLM's whole KV cache into /dev/shm, so SHM_SIZE must exceed KV_CACHE_GB. The default so the lane exercises the shared-memory IPC path TRANSFER_MODE=engine_driven works — 0.191 s and 0.050 s, inline over ZMQ, no shared memory TRANSFER_MODE=auto works; the worker picks engine_driven LMCACHE_USE_UPSTREAM_MP=1 dies at startup: TypeError: LMCacheMPSchedulerAdapter.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'server_url' server lmcache_driven, worker auto dies at startup: LMCache server rejected RPC 'register_kv_cache_engine_driven_context' (operation_not_enabled)

The last row is why one variable sets the mode on both services.

docs.title: Running It
docs.text:
make cpu-load                    # vllm-cpu and lmcache-cpu, into the local daemon
make cpu-serve                   # compose up on THIS machine, port 8000
make cpu-logs CPU_LOG_ARGS='-f vllm'
make cpu-down
make cpu-test CPU_TEST_ARGS=--l2 # its own project and port (8012)

BUILDER defaults to a fleet builder; off the fleet, pass your own. The compose file owns the runtime defaults, the model included (HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct; CPU_SERVE_MODEL= overrides it). The ones worth knowing: KV_TIER=cpu|file, TRANSFER_MODE, KV_CACHE_GB (1 — unset, vLLM sizes the KV cache from 92% of RAM, its default --gpu-memory-utilization; read from source, not measured), KV_OFFLOAD=0 for a no-connector baseline, VLLM_EXTRA_ARGS, and CPUSET / VLLM_MEM_LIMIT / LMCACHE_MEM_LIMIT to make a large machine look like a 4 vCPU runner. With the defaults: vLLM 3.7–3.9 GiB, LMCache about 1.4 GiB, 67–76 s to healthy on four cores of an AVX-512 host. VLLM_EXTRA_ARGS=--enforce-eager cuts that to 27 s and puts a ~5 s kernel compile on the first request.

docs.title: On The Serving Host
docs.text:
Those rules use this machine's docker daemon, which is what CI and a laptop have. The serve-* rules run the same compose file on GPU_HOST instead, over DOCKER_HOST=ssh://, when given SERVE_DEVICE=cpu:

make serve-stack SERVE_DEVICE=cpu VLLM_DEV_MODE=1 \
     KV_TIER=file KV_STORE=/mnt/kv-nvme/rocm-bake-l2
make serve-test  SERVE_DEVICE=cpu    # also serve-test-l2, serve-test-baseline
make serve-logs
make serve-down  SERVE_DEVICE=cpu
  • Pass it to every rule. The CPU stack is its own compose project, rocm-serving-cpu, so serve-down without it stops the ROCm one. VLLM_PORT=8001 moves it off the ROCm stack's port 8000 (serve-wait run on its own needs that too), but take the CPU stack down before running the ROCm serve-test*: serve-test.sh picks LMCache containers by name, so it would read the CPU stack's log and, for serve-test-l2, try to clear the CPU stack's L1.
  • Nothing is asked of the host's GPU. No /dev/kfd probe, no rocminfo: the tags are ${VLLM_REF}-cpu and ${LMCACHE_REF}-cpu, and the model is this compose file's default unless SERVE_MODEL= says otherwise.
  • It pulls before it serves, and stops if it cannot. The compose file has no pull_policy because CI loads its images, so a served host would otherwise keep its first image for good. SERVE_PULL=0 serves images loaded onto the host by hand.
  • serve-stack replaces a running CPU stack, down then up, once the pull has succeeded. vLLM's KV segment sits in LMCache's /dev/shm and outlives a recreated vllm; up on a live stack left one behind each time, and the third start died with Insufficient space in /dev/shm. Settings are not remembered: repeat KV_TIER, KV_STORE and the rest on every serve-stack.
  • serve-test is cpu-test.sh --attach, not serve-test.sh. It runs the checks below against the stack already up, reading the containers through docker on the host, and starts and stops nothing. A host or a project it cannot find is a failure, not a skip.
  • The cache check needs VLLM_DEV_MODE=1 on the stack, passed to serve-stack, not to serve-test, and fails saying so without it. serve-test-baseline, for a stack from serve-vllm, skips the cache checks; serve-test-l2 needs KV_TIER=file and empties LMCache's L1. KV_TIER on a serve-test* line is ignored: the tier is read from the stack.
  • emu-capture-* refuse: a capture records a card.

docs.title: What The Test Checks
docs.text:
.builders/cpu-test.sh starts the stack, tests it and removes it (--keep, --l2, --baseline, --attach PROJECT, --endpoint URL). /health and a non-empty completion only prove the HTTP stack is up, so the checks that matter are the later ones:

Check What it proves cpu prints this host's ISA flags first, so a SIGILL is attributable health, models, completion the server is up and serving the model asked for inference a temperature-0 question is answered correctly, and the log shows weights were loaded same-server with --attach: the container found through docker is the one that answered — its access log carries this run's tag. Otherwise --endpoint at another stack of the same model passes isa which vllm/_C*.abi3.so the engine actually mapped no-device no CUDA or HIP in torch, no /dev/kfd, no /dev/dri cache a repeated prefix is served from LMCache with vLLM's own prefix cache emptied; the answer and every logprob match; LMCache logged the store and the retrieve l2 with --l2: the file tier holds the blocks and serves them with L1 emptied

The cache check compares the LMCache answer against the one from vLLM's own prefix cache, not against the first, computed one. Computed and cached answers differed on 8 of 130 prompts on 32 threads with nothing wrong; own-cache against LMCache was bit-identical 100 of 100. With KV_OFFLOAD=0 the check fails, as it should; --baseline says that was the intent and skips it.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
cpu.yml builds both wheels and both images on a stock hosted runner and runs cpu-test.sh. Its first run passed 11 of 11 and took 33 minutes, 22 of them the vLLM compile and 2 the 120 s startup on 4 vCPUs. That is the cold case. What keeps a pull request off it:

  • The compile is a cache read when nothing under it moved. The wheel builder stages are cached in the Actions cache, one scope per Dockerfile.
  • Pull requests start from main's cache. A pull request can read the cache its base branch wrote, and one written from a pull request is visible to that pull request alone. So the push to main is what warms everyone, and a pull request's own cache only helps its next push.
  • A daily scheduled run on main reads that cache, which keeps it inside the Actions cache's seven-day eviction.
  • The manylinux base is a dated tag. :latest was republished eleven times in three weeks, each one a new digest under the builder stage and a cold compile for whichever pull request came next. MANYLINUX_IMAGE now moves only when someone bumps it.

A warm run took 5 min 46 s, with the wheel step down from 27 minutes to 4 seconds. That run served with --enforce-eager and wrote no cache; the workflow as it stands does neither, so expect a minute or two more. It serves in the default mode because eager skips the warmup compile of the backbone outright, and the pull requests that run this workflow are the ones that can break it.

A pull request is still cold, about half an hour, on its first push when it changes something under the compile: the vLLM builder stage, VLLM_REF, PYTORCH_VERSION or MANYLINUX_IMAGE. Its later pushes read the cache that first one wrote.

docs.title: Installing From The cpu Index
docs.text:
make push-cpu           # the whole group; the only rule that pushes both wheels
make cpu-index          # fetch from Zot, build the PEP 503 index
make cpu-index-check    # install it in a throwaway venv, refuse any nvidia-*
make cpu-publish-dry
make cpu-publish

Not published yet: the URL below is where make cpu-publish will put it, and it returns 404 until then.

The index carries vLLM and LMCache and no torch. Two steps, with pip:

pip install --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu "torch==2.15.0+cpu"

pip install \
  --index-url https://sbates130272.github.io/rocm-bake/data/wheels/cpu/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu \
  "rocm-torch[device-cpu]"
  • Pass both extra indexes. The vLLM wheel requires torch==2.15.0+cpu plus torchvision, torchaudio and torchcodec, and their CPU builds are on PyTorch's index only. With torch already installed pip does not stop without it: it resolves and takes PyPI's builds of those three instead, which this lane has not tested. Only with step one skipped as well does it fail, at Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement torch==2.15.0+cpu.
  • Install through the metapackage, or pin both wheels yourself in one command. An unpinned vllm resolves to PyPI's newer CUDA build and its nvidia-* stack.
  • The metapackage is still called rocm-torch. The name and its ROCm-derived version come from the shared publishing machinery. rocm-torch[device-cpu] pins vllm==0.33.0+cpu and lmcache==0.5.7+cpu; nothing in either contains or needs ROCm.
  • uv refuses it. vLLM's CPU requirements name triton-cpu by direct URL, kept as upstream has it. pip fetches it from github.com; uv 0.13.8 stops with Package triton was included as a URL dependency.

It has its own index for the reason emu does: vllm 0.33.0+cpu must never sit beside vllm 0.33.0+rocm101.

docs.title: What It Does Not Tell You
docs.text:
• Nothing about performance. No number on this page is a benchmark. The timings came from a shared host and say nothing about a GPU or about this repo's ROCm stack.
  • The AVX2 path has not run on AVX2-only hardware. _C_AVX2 loaded and computed one op under qemu-x86_64 -cpu EPYC-Milan, and served end to end with the CPUID selection forced on an AVX-512 host. Every real run here mapped vllm/_C.abi3.so. The first hosted runner without AVX-512 is the confirmation; cpu-test.sh prints which variant it got.
  • CI has run it twice, both on hosts with AVX-512. Both hosted runs landed on an EPYC 9V74 that exposes avx512f and avx512_bf16, so they too mapped vllm/_C.abi3.so. The workflow as it stands, see In CI, has not itself been timed warm.
  • SERVE_DEVICE=cpu has run on one serving host. serve-stack and serve-test-l2 passed all 14 checks against snoc-thinkstation over DOCKER_HOST=ssh://, file tier on a dedicated NVMe. That host has AVX-512, like every other machine this lane has run on.
  • The model is tiny. 135M parameters and one checkable question. That proves weights load and tokens are real, not that a model you care about fits or is usable on CPU.
  • Bit-identical logprobs held on one model, on AVX-512. Unverified on AVX2 or anything else. If vLLM's own prefix cache is disabled the same-answer check reports SKIP, not FAIL.
  • Nothing about the connector on a GPU. The bare connector name resolving to LMCache's class was measured on CPU only.
  • Nothing has been published. push-cpu, cpu-index and cpu-publish have not been run; the index check's recipe passed by hand against this lane's wheels in a container, not through make.
  • Unverified: reproducibility of the two wheels; LMCACHE_USE_UPSTREAM_MP=1 with lmcache_driven; the reduced op set upstream documents for AVX2 hosts (read from source, not exercised); Docker Engine older than 25, which lacks the healthchecks' start_interval.

docs.title: Emulated Serving: One vLLM Wheel, No GPU
docs.text:
Every ROCm vLLM artifact here is welded to one card. The HIP extensions carry code objects for a single architecture, so gfx950 and gfx1201 need separate wheels, separate indexes and separate releases — and a machine with no supported AMD GPU can install none of them.

This lane builds the other kind: one wheel for every architecture, with no device code at all, and an emulator that makes it still serve.

make push-emu BUILDER=snoc-pool    # build and publish both targets
make emu-load && make emu-test     # serve a model and prove it emulated

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Two things, built together by docker/Dockerfile.vllm-emu:

vLLM with no backend. VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=empty takes setup.py down its _no_device() path — no CMake, no HIP, no CUDA, requirements collapsed to requirements/common.txt, and the version suffixed +empty. The result contains no compiled code at all, so it ships as py3-none-any: not merely independent of the card, independent of the machine.

That is one better than intended. The aim was a manylinux wheel, on the theory that setup.py's Rust frontend extension would be the one piece of native code left. It is not: that extension is built with optional=not should_require_rust_frontend() and VLLM_REQUIRE_RUST_FRONTEND is unset, so it is skipped — and it is opt-in at runtime too (VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND defaults to 0; only --grpc-port and vllm bench serve consult it). Forcing it to build would buy an unused feature at the cost of pinning the wheel to x86_64. The build decides the tag by looking inside the archive rather than asserting it, and keeps the auditwheel path for the day upstream makes the extension mandatory.

LLM-Emu. A profile-driven emulator, from the MLArchSys@ISCA poster of the same name. It replaces vLLM's GPU forward pass with a latency draw from a profile pack captured once on real hardware. The scheduler, HTTP stack, admission control, tokenizer and output pipeline are vLLM's own code, running unmodified. Weights are never materialised — GPUModelRunner.load_model is stubbed — so nothing is downloaded beyond a model's config and tokenizer, and nothing is allocated on a device that is not there.

The result serves. It schedules, batches, admits, streams, and answers /v1/completions, on any x86 box.

docs.title: Why This Repo Wants It
docs.text:
Three things it buys:

A serving lane that can actually be exercised. No node on the fleet currently has a usable GPU. vllm's verification stops at "it imports"; atom-vllm ships with its plugin disabled and says so. This and the CPU lane are the only serving artifacts in the repo that are tested end to end, and both tests run in CI, on a free runner, before anything is published. See .github/workflows/emu.yml.

An installable vLLM for machines without AMD hardware. Laptops, CI, a developer reading the scheduler. Published under its own index; see below.

A scheduler and serving-stack testbed. Admission policy, batching behaviour, queueing under load — all of that is vLLM's real code here, and all of it is observable without a card.

docs.title: What It Does Not Tell You
docs.text:
Worth being blunt, because the output looks like a benchmark:

  • It is not a measurement of this repo's stack. The emulated device presents as an AMD Instinct MI455X — 432 GiB of HBM4 and 256 CDNA 5 compute units, AMD's published figures — but every latency in the pack was captured on an NVIDIA A40. The pack is relabelled, not re-measured, and says so in its own rocm_bake_provenance block. Nothing in it tells you anything about MI455X, gfx1250, our PyTorch, our AITER or our Triton. More accurate estimates are expected later; until then these are placeholders.
  • The memory figure is a datasheet number, not a measured one. A real device reports less than its nominal capacity once ECC and firmware reservations come out — the A40 this pack came from is a 48 GiB card reporting 47,709,159,424 bytes, which is 44.43 GiB, or 92.6%. So the KV cache sized from 432 GiB is optimistic, and rocminfo should replace it as soon as anyone has the part.
  • No kernel runs. There is nothing here to profile, optimise or regress. A faster kernel changes nothing a run reports.
  • No accuracy signal. The emulator emits a fixed filler token. The text coming back is not model output and is not meant to be read. CPU serving is the complement: real weights and real tokens on the same GPU-free footing, and no latency claim at all.
  • Fidelity is the pack's, not ours. Upstream reports TPOT and ITL within ~1% of real runs and TTFT within ~10% at low request rates — for the model and hardware a pack was captured on. Serving a model the pack does not describe is extrapolation.

A pack measured on one of this repo's own targets has to be captured there, from a real vLLM on a real GPU. The tooling for that exists; no such pack has been captured yet. See Capturing a pack.

docs.title: The shipped pack is reduced
docs.text:
Upstream's file is 11 MB; the one in the image is 836 KB. Half of that saving is lossless: step_cycle_2d_distribution is a verbatim duplicate of the prefill and decode tables merged — 46,166 + 232,234 = 278,400 samples — and the oracle never reads it while both of those exist. The build refuses to drop it when they do not.

The rest is quantisation. Each bucket keeps 64 quantiles of itself rather than all 556,800 raw measurements, which samples the same distribution: the oracle draws with random.choice(), so a uniform draw over evenly spaced quantiles is inverse-transform sampling of the empirical CDF. Min and max are preserved exactly, so the tails survive. Measured over 20,000 draws per query against the original, medians agree within 0.01% on the common decode buckets; the worst case is −0.75% on the median and +2.47% at p95, on the heaviest prefill bucket.

64 is not arbitrary. Adaptive-K pooling grows its neighbourhood until the cumulative sample count reaches VLLM_EMULATOR_ORACLE_MIN_SAMPLES — default 30 — and counts len(samples), so anything at or above that floor leaves pooling decisions unchanged. Below it, the oracle would quietly start merging neighbouring batch shapes.

docs.title: Two known defects in the emulator's output
docs.text:
Found by audit rather than by hitting them, both in LLM-Emu's executor hook, both non-fatal and both invisible to a short smoke test. Neither is fixed yet; they are recorded here so results are not read as cleaner than they are.

Chunked prefill emits a phantom token. The hook decides which requests are mid-prefill by iterating scheduled_new_reqs only, so chunks 2..n of a long prompt — which arrive in scheduled_cached_reqs — are treated as decode steps and get a filler token appended. A prompt longer than the per-step token budget therefore accumulates extra output tokens mid-prefill, and can reach max_tokens or a stop check early. Short prompts never hit it.

Logprobs rows are indexed against the wrong batch. The hook builds its LogprobsLists arrays with one row per request that produced a token, while vLLM's scheduler indexes them by position in the full batch. With logprobs requested and any request mid-prefill in the same step, rows are attributed to the wrong requests.

docs.title: How The Wiring Works
docs.text:
LLM-Emu ships its vLLM integration as a unified diff against vLLM 0.18.1; this repo pins v0.34.0. Measured against v0.33.0, the pin at the time, five of seven hunks in vllm/v1/engine/core.py and one of four in vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py fail to apply, and the scheduler.py hunk turns out to add an unused import and two blank lines. Upstream says as much: regenerating the patch is expected on every vLLM bump.

Doing that each time is what this repo avoids. Instead docker/vllm-emu-shim/ applies the wiring to vLLM's classes at plugin-load time, through the same meta-path import hook LLM-Emu already uses for GPUModelRunner and gpu_worker in cuda_mock.py. Nothing patches vLLM's source, so a VLLM_REF bump cannot leave a stale diff behind.

It also turns out to need far less than the diff carries. Of ~170 patched lines, about 25 matter for emulation:

What Where attach the executor hook UniProcExecutor.__init__ hand the step to the oracle UniProcExecutor.execute_model return the oracle's pending Future UniProcExecutor.sample_tokens release it UniProcExecutor.shutdown survive an empty batch EngineCore.step_with_batch_queue

The rest is StepCycleTracer instrumentation for capturing a pack on a real GPU, which we consume rather than produce.

The third row is not cosmetic: the async engine needs a pending Future while the next batch is scheduled, so the hook's timer Future has to reach the engine rather than a resolved stand-in.

docs.title: When vLLM moves
docs.text: The shim makes assumptions — that those methods still take non_block, that EngineCore still raises RuntimeError("unexpected error") on the empty-batch path. Assumptions in a comment are facts about one day, so vllm-emu-selftest re-measures each of them, the same way docker/wheel-verdict.py re-measures the manylinux verdicts. It runs inside the image build and again at the top of make emu-test, so a bump that invalidates one fails loudly rather than serving wrongly.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
One index per device, named emu-<gfx>, each with its own release:

make emu-index          # fetch from Zot, build a PEP 503 index per device
make emu-index-check    # install each in a throwaway venv and import it
make emu-publish-dry
make emu-publish        # a release and a gh-pages index per device
index pack timings emu-gfx1151 vllm-emu-pack-gfx1151 measured on an AMD Radeon 8060S emu-gfx1250 vllm-emu-pack-gfx1250 an NVIDIA A40's, relabelled

One pack per index, and that is a constraint rather than a convention. The shim uses a pack only when exactly one is installed, and the generated rocm-torch metapackage pins every wheel in its index — so an index carrying two packs resolves to a server that comes up on LLM-Emu's fallback device. The wheel image builds every pack; make emu-index drops the ones each index must not carry, and narrows wheels-arch.txt to match so wheelindex.py still checks the directory against something true.

Not the plain gfx names. data/wheels/gfx1151/ is the ROCm wheel index for that card. Putting vllm 0.33.0+empty beside vllm 0.33.0+rocm10.1.0 is the collision this lane exists to avoid, one directory further down.

docs.title: Installing from it needs a torch
docs.text:
The index does not contain one, and the metapackage does not pin one:

rocm-torch 10.1.0+emu-gfx1151.<digest>  (extra: device-emu-gfx1151)
  llm-emu==0.1.0
  vllm==0.33.0+empty
  vllm-emu-shim==0.1.0
  vllm-emu-pack-gfx1151==0.1.0+<ref>

vLLM built with VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=empty resolves its dependencies from requirements/common.txt, which names no torch at all, so nothing drags one in behind the metapackage. Installing it alone gives you a vLLM that cannot import vllm.

(The fourth wheel is the profile pack.
